instagram_media.caption:
Why old Indian houses had a hole in the middle

The aangan, the open courtyard at the heart of many old Indian homes, was not just for family life. In a 250-year-old haveli in Bikaner, researchers logged 45°C outside on 21 June. The courtyard itself reached 43°C, but the bedroom beside it never went above 30°C, with no AC.

Three things did it:
1. Shade: a small, deep courtyard with a sunshade on top keeps the rooms around it in shade.
2. Thick walls: about 70 cm of wall delays the heat by about 10 hours, so it arrives at night when the air outside is cooler.
3. Airflow: the courtyard is the only way air gets in, so it keeps moving.

Would you give up one room for a hole in the middle?

instagram_media.caption:
Hong Kong homes smaller than a parking space

About 2.2 lakh people in Hong Kong live in subdivided flats: one old apartment cut into tiny rooms. The typical room is about 110 sq ft, smaller than a 135 sq ft parking space, and rents for about ₹55,000 a month. Yet only about 7% of Hong Kong's land has homes on it and about 40% is protected country park. Delhi packs in more people per sq km. Since March 2026 a new law sets a minimum of 8 sq m (about 86 sq ft) with a window, and about 70% of these flats had registered by October.

Why Kerala has lakhs of locked, empty houses

The 2011 Census counted about 11.9 lakh vacant houses in Kerala, about one in ten, and over 3 lakh of them had four or more rooms. About 22 lakh Keralites live abroad, most in the Gulf, and in 2023 they sent home over ₹2 lakh crore. Much of that money builds a big house back home, while the next generation often moves away too. Pathanamthitta alone has over 61,000 closed homes, and in 2023 the state proposed a tax on locked houses, then dropped it within a month.

instagram_media.caption:
Paying EMIs for a flat that never came? The Supreme Court stepped in twice on 19 Nov 2026.

Sonipat: buyers had a three-way (tripartite) loan deal with the builder and the bank. The project stalled and the builder went into insolvency. The court said there can be no coercive recovery from the buyers until the commercial court checks whether they really defaulted and whether the bank released the loan to the builder as the agreement said. In a three-way loan, the money is meant to go in stages as the building rises.

Bengaluru: about 4,500 buyers of a stalled project in insolvency, who had paid about 95% of the price, get no coercive measures till they receive their flats. The court also said such buyers should go to the High Court or NCLT first.

instagram_media.caption:
The South Mumbai flat that rented for about ₹1,300 a month

In 2012 Bloomberg reported a family paying about ₹1,300 a month for a 2,600 sq ft flat on Nepean Sea Road, where market rent was over ₹1 lakh. The reason: Bombay's 1947 rent law froze rents at 1940 levels, and the 1999 Act allows only small yearly increases. Researchers found controlled rent can be one-thousandth of market rent. Landlords stop repairing, about 14,000 old cessed buildings age, and yet tenancies change hands for pagdi worth about 80% of ownership value. When that building was redeveloped, the tenants were paid about ₹14 crore to move. (Rupee figures converted from Bloomberg's figures at the 2012 rate.)

Property prices never fall? US home prices fell 34%.

The S&P Case-Shiller 10-City index fell 34% between April 2006 and January 2012, and in 2014 it was still below the peak. In China, new home prices were still falling in October 2026, down 2.4% in a year. In India, the RBI House Price Index rose 3.6% in the year to April to June 2026, while retail inflation was 4.38% in June. Prices can fall, stall or trail inflation, and every city moves differently. Check the index, not the brochure.

Why is Jaipur pink? 1876, a royal welcome, and a law that followed.

Jaipur was founded on 18 November 1727 as one of India's earliest planned cities, laid out on a grid. In 1876 Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II had the old city painted pink, a colour of welcome, for the visiting Prince of Wales. A law in 1877 is said to have made pink compulsory there. In 2017 the city's smart city plan set aside about ₹14.6 crore to restore bazaar facades in the original colour, and in 2019 UNESCO listed the walled city as a World Heritage Site. Some historians think the city was pinkish even before, and 1876 was a repaint.

instagram_media.caption:
Jakarta is sinking, and the sea is not the main reason

Parts of North Jakarta have sunk up to 25 cm in a year, and some areas dropped about 2.5 m in 10 years. The main cause researchers name: groundwater. Homes and factories pump water from wells under their own floors, the soft clay below dries out and compacts, and the city drops with it. About 40% of Jakarta already sits below sea level, and coastal streets now live behind sea walls.

Indonesia's answer: build a new capital. Nusantara, in East Kalimantan on Borneo, more than 1,200 km away. Construction began in 2022. It is planned for about 1.2 million people by 2029, at an expected cost of about USD 45 billion. As of October 2026, about 10,000 people have moved in.

Fix the sinking city, or build a new one? Which would you pick?

Delhi to Mumbai Expressway: promised by 2024, still being built in 2026

929 of 1,445 km was open as of March 2026, about 64%. It has opened one stretch at a time: Sohna to Dausa in Feb 2023, the MP section in Sep 2023, Vadodara to Bharuch in Feb 2024, Kota to Laban in Dec 2024, Bharuch to Kharel in Jan 2026 and Limkheda to Godhra in Oct 2026.

Delhi to Vadodara missed its June 2026 target. About 30 km near the MP border is now due Dec 2026 or Jan 2027, and the last packages near Maharashtra by March 2028. Sanctioned cost: ₹96,547 crore, of which ₹77,558 crore (about 80%) was spent by Dec 2025.

When a brochure says "minutes from the expressway", check which stretch is actually open.

Why so many Indian houses have steel rods sticking out of the roof

Those rods are the tops of the columns, left there on purpose. Many Indian homes are built floor by floor, as money comes in. Leave the rods out and the next floor's columns can lock into the old ones. Cut them off, and later someone has to drill into the columns and glue new bars in.

The catch: bare steel rusts, and rust can take up to six times the volume of the steel it eats. Rain running down the rods into the column can crack the concrete from the inside.
